content: 1. Rowley et al. (2019) conducted a study to estimate the global prevalence and incidence of four major sexually transmitted infections (STIs): chlamydia, gonorrhea, trichomoniasis, and syphilis, using data from 2016. The findings were published in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization. 2. Van Boeckel et al. (2014) analyzed global antibiotic consumption trends from 2000 to 2010 by examining national pharmaceutical sales data. Their study, published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases, highlighted significant increases in antibiotic use worldwide. 3. Korenromp et al. (2017) evaluated the costs associated with implementing national STI programs as part of the global STI control strategy for the health sector between 2016 and 2021. Their findings were published in PLoS One. 4. Okuku et al. (2012) assessed the effectiveness of presumptive treatment recommendations for asymptomatic anorectal gonorrhea and chlamydia infections in at-risk men who have sex with men (MSM) in Kenya. The study was published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society. 5. Annex 7 provides a decision-making framework for managing anorectal discharge, including risk assessment based on unprotected anal intercourse, STI exposure, and multiple partners. It outlines follow-up protocols and treatment options for conditions such as lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) and herpes simplex virus (HSV). 6. Mugundu et al. (2008–2009) conducted a study in India involving 868 MSM recruited from sexual health clinics. They used proctoscopy and smear findings to define positive cases of anorectal syndromes caused by Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Diagnostic testing was performed using Roche Amplicor NAAT, yielding 53 true positives, 74 false negatives, 250 false positives, and 491 true negatives. 7. Quilter et al. (date unclear) studied 698 MSM in Kenya, using a model-derived risk score to assess anorectal symptoms. Testing with Abbott RealTime NAAT identified 15 true positives, 21 false negatives, 151 false positives, and 511 true negatives. 8. Rebe et al. (2012) conducted a study in South Africa involving 200 MSM from sexual health clinics. They used symptoms alone to define cases of anorectal syndromes caused by C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae. Testing with Aptima Combo yielded 29 true positives, 38 false negatives, 13 false positives, and 140 true negatives. 9. Sanders et al. (2011–2012) studied 244 MSM in Kenya, combining symptoms and risk assessment to define cases. Testing with Aptima Combo identified 23 true positives, 28 false negatives, 1 false positive, and 212 true negatives. 10. Annex 8 focuses on the detection of anal gonorrhea and chlamydia in anorectal syndromes. It includes data from studies in Brazil, Peru, Kenya, and South Africa, highlighting diagnostic performance metrics such as true positives, false negatives, false positives, and true negatives for various subpopulations, including MSM and trans women.
